name: How Much Contingency Should I Budget for an Older San Diego Kitchen?

mainEntity.name: What hidden problems should I budget for when renovating a kitchen in an older San Diego home?
mainEntity.text: What hidden problems should I budget for when renovating a kitchen in an older San Diego home?

acceptedAnswer.text: A contingency protects the project from conditions that cannot be confirmed before demolition. In older San Diego homes, possible discoveries include deteriorated supply or drain lines, outdated electrical systems, insufficient circuits, unlevel floors, water-damaged cabinet bases, weak subfloors, hidden framing, and inadequate ventilation. The likelihood depends on the home’s age, maintenance history, and prior remodeling. Ask for a preconstruction inspection and have the contractor identify areas that cannot be verified without opening walls or floors. Request separate budget ranges for likely upgrades such as electrical circuits, plumbing repairs, floor leveling, drywall replacement, and structural adjustments. Keep contingency funds separate from appliance and finish allowances so a surprise repair does not force lower-quality selections. The contract should require photos, a written explanation, and a price and schedule impact before concealed-condition work proceeds, except for urgent safety measures. Avoid approving broad verbal change orders. A realistic budget includes permits, delivery, disposal, temporary kitchen costs, finish repairs, and final inspection corrections—not only cabinets, counters, and labor.
acceptedAnswer.description: Older kitchens may reveal outdated wiring, weak plumbing, uneven floors, water damage, poor ventilation, unlevel walls, damaged subfloors, or concealed framing changes. Set aside a project contingency after defining the scope, and ask the contractor to price likely upgrades separately. Do not spend the entire budget on visible finishes before opening critical areas.
